articles.title: Entertainment television and a wildlife documentary produce equal engagement but opposite conservation behavior
articles.authors: Alexandra Boren, Diogo Veríssimo, Chase Alexander Niesner, Jiaying Zhao, Nicolas Ara, Alejandra Echeverri
articles.abstract: Entertainment media reaches billions of people and shapes how they understand the natural world, yet its consequences for real conservation behavior remain largely untested. Because mainstream entertainment often reaches broader audiences than conservation documentaries, it may shape pro-wildlife attitudes and behaviors as powerfully as explicitly educational media. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned participants (n=400) to view an episode of a wildlife conservation documentary (Blue Planet II) or a commercial fishing reality television program (Wicked Tuna), both portraying the same marine domain through opposing narratives. Using multi-group structural equation modeling, we show that the front end of narrative persuasion operated equivalently across programs: narrative transportation predicted character identification, which predicted attitude toward the episode, and identification extended even to non-charismatic fish. This shared engagement then diverged sharply at attitude formation: greater engagement with Wicked Tuna produced a more instrumental view of human-fish relationships, whereas Blue Planet II did not. These attitudinal effects were associated with a divergence in behavior. Signing a program-congruent petition, rather than the experimental condition itself, most strongly predicted which charity participants donated real money to, consistent with a small public commitment channeling a narrative-induced identity into costly action. Notably, pro-fish attitudes mobilized donations most strongly among viewers whose media was not already conservation-branded. Narrative engagement therefore carries limited intrinsic conservation valence, and its effects depend on the protagonist and perspective an audience is given. Reaching non-self-selected audiences through identity-matched entertainment may yield larger behavioral gains than intensifying appeals to audiences already primed toward conservation.

articles.title: Sustainable Transport and Urban Inequality: A Mixed Methods Study of Selective Siting and Procedural Justice in Berlin
articles.authors: Katja Salomo, Sarah George, Vanessa Rösner, Viktoria Scheidler

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Urban sustainability policies are widely promoted as key instruments for mitigating climate change and improving urban quality of life. At the same time, concerns have grown that such interventions may reproduce socio spatial inequalities through selec-tive siting, uneven benefits, and exclusionary planning processes. This paper examines both the distribution and lived experience of sustainable transport measures, combining a citywide spatial analysis with a qualitative neighborhood case study. Using 1 km × 1 km grid level data for Berlin, we analyze the socio economic correlates of multiple transport sustainability measures, including ride sharing stations, EV charging points, cycling infrastructure, traffic calming measures, and low traffic zones. Spatially Lagged X (SLX) models reveal policy specific patterns: infrastructure ena-bling alternative modes of transport tends to cluster in and around more affluent but also, in some cases, more diverse neighborhoods, while grids with higher child poverty are systematically less likely to feature traffic calmed street space. Low traffic zones are more prevalent in affluent areas, too. Complementary focus group discussions conducted during the implementation of a low-traffic zone show that residents from diverse and poorer neighborhoods as well as small business owners frequently interpret such street space interventions through the lens of gentrification and displacement. Participants describe feelings of alienation and criticize unclear communication and tokenistic participation. Our findings suggest that gentrification concerns may become a significant barrier to public support for urban sustainability transitions.

articles.title: Clarifying the governance of solar geoengineering experiments: lessons from health-related hazards within a multi-hazard approach
articles.authors: Guillermo Marín Penella, Timothy Daly, Ignacio Mastroleo
articles.abstract: Priority Two of the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) Sendai Framework recognises the need to strengthen disaster risk governance to manage disaster risk. Focusing specifically on Priority Two of the UNDRR framework, we expand the “multi-hazard approach” to include the formulation of a ‘lesson transfer’ heuristic that encourages the application of governance lessons across different types of hazards. We take as examples the governance controversies associated with recent small-scale solar geoengineering experiments, and show how drawing a fundamental aim-based distinction between research and non-research experiments, which has its roots in the governance of health-related hazards, can reduce confusion about how to govern outdoor geoengineering experiments. We develop further the research/non-research distinction through the concepts of validated practice and non-validated practice, and discuss how it maps onto the concept of ‘emergency.’ The concepts mobilised are then applied to the specific case of Stratospheric Aerosol Injection (SAI), a form of solar geoengineering, to illustrate different categories in need of distinct ethical and governance mechanisms.

articles.title: Political Science: Concepts, Branches, and Its Role in Society
articles.abstract: Political science is an important branch of the social sciences that studies power, the state, government, political institutions, political behavior, and relations among states. Understanding political science is not important only for students of the discipline; it is also useful for citizens who want to understand their society and political environment more clearly. This paper aims to introduce the concept of political science, explain its importance, examine its major branches, and discuss its role in society. The study uses a descriptive-analytical approach based mainly on documentary and library research.

articles.title: Does Power-Sharing Reduce Polarization and Improve Performance? Evidence from the Tunisian Parliament
articles.abstract: Power-sharing arrangements like grand coalitions and unity governments are often touted as a way for transitional democracies to reduce political tensions and improve government performance. Yet there are few empirical tests of their effectiveness. We theorize that power-sharing is more likely to incentivize postponing polarizing issues, rather than resolving them, delaying the necessary but controversial reforms in order to preserve the coalition. We test this hypothesis in the case of Tunisia, which had been considered the Arab Spring's success story for its pursuit of power-sharing. To measure polarization, we examine all roll call votes from Tunisia's first and second post-transition parliaments (2011-2019). Employing a time-varying ideal point model, we show that power-sharing merely masked polarization, while also postponing critical political and economic reforms. The case of Tunisia suggests that even in homogeneous countries with voluntary grand coalitions, power-sharing is no panacea for a bitterly divided polity.

articles.title: The Price of Opportunity: School Quality and Housing Prices in the Dayton Metropolitan Area
articles.abstract: This study examines the relationship between school performance and housing prices in the Dayton Metropolitan Area. The analysis uses data from 40 geographic subunits across seven school districts, combining housing prices, Ohio Performance Index scores, and socioeconomic characteristics. A baseline regression is first used to estimate the association between school performance and housing prices while controlling for socioeconomic characteristics, followed by a district fixed-effects model that accounts for unobserved characteristics shared by geographic subunits within the same school district. The baseline model finds a positive and statistically significant association, with a one-point higher Performance Index associated with approximately 1.8% higher median home prices. However, after the district fixed effects are included, the Performance Index coefficient becomes negative and statistically insignificant. This indicates that the positive association does not remain within districts under this specification. These findings suggest that the observed relationship between school performance and housing prices may reflect broader differences across school districts rather than a consistent relationship within districts.

articles.title: Coltivare identità: il ruolo della passione del tutor di tirocinio nello sviluppo dell'identità professionale dello studente infermiere. Una revisione sistematica della letteratura [Cultivating identity: the role of the clinical tutor's passion in the development of the nursing student's professional identity. A systematic literature review]
articles.authors: Mariagrazia Salonna, Letizia Nava, Arturo Conte
articles.abstract: Background and aim: Clinical placement is the setting in which nursing students build their professional identity, and the clinical tutor is their main role model. The literature mostly describes the behavioural and organisational aspects of this role, overlooking its affective and motivational dimension. This review aimed to explore the role of the clinical tutor's passion in the development of nursing students' professional identity. Methods: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, with a research question structured according to the PICO framework. In April 2026, CINAHL, Scopus, ERIC, PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched (studies in Italian or English, 2010-2026). Methodological quality was appraised with design-specific tools and findings were integrated through Thomas and Harden's thematic synthesis. Results: Of 8,476 records identified, 61 studies were included, mostly qualitative and of moderate quality. Five analytical themes emerged: the tutor's passion as a mechanism for transmitting professional identity, effective when combined with good relational quality; a continuum ranging from transformative passion to bullying and incivility; the moderating role of placement organisation; the multifactorial nature of identity development; the lack of instruments directly measuring the tutor's passion. Conclusions: The tutor's passion is a facilitating condition, but not the only driver of professional identity development. Tutor education programmes focused on relational competence and dedicated measurement instruments are needed. Original contribution: the review develops new analytical themes through thematic synthesis, reframes the tutor's influence as a continuum of affective-relational quality, identifies the absence of instruments measuring tutors' passion as a research gap, and interprets the findings through social learning theory, professional socialisation models and the philosophy of care. Undergraduate thesis in Nursing, University of Modena and Reggio Emilia (academic year 2025/2026), written in Italian with an English abstract. Review registration (retrospective): https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/NHQW2

articles.title: The Ubiquitous Sphoṭa Pratibhā Model of Consciousness Centred Communication
articles.abstract: The Ubiquitous Sphoṭa–Pratibhā model develops consciousness centred communication through Indian philosophical principles. It takes the situated meaning episode as its unit of analysis and explains communication through relations between lived apprehension, formulation, public expression, uptake and revision. Its conceptual centre is the apprehension of the import of an expression encountered as a linguistic whole. Sphoṭa and pratibhā identify the structural and apprehensive aspects of this episode. Bhartṛhari supplies this centre; Pratyabhijñā distinguishes intrinsic reflexivity from deliberate reflection; Nyāya informs the scrutiny of cognition and its grounds; Sanskrit poetics explains the reach of suggestion and aesthetic experience. The model advances five theoretical principles concerning situated apprehension, generative formulation, coordination without identity of interpretation, consequential return and differentiated achievement. It connects the participant’s experience of meaning with the public commitments through which communication acquires consequences. Experienced intelligibility, demonstrated grasp, articulation, coordination, warrant and fidelity to documented human intention require distinct evidence. Their divergence explains how communication can produce fluent expression, agreement or a completed task while leaving understanding or justification unresolved. An asymmetric human–AI architecture extends the account without assigning human experiential structures to computational systems. Four prospective propositions specify empirical tests and conditions of failure. USP contributes a philosophical and theoretical account of how meaning becomes intelligible to participants, takes public form and returns through encounters that can transform both understanding and action.Keywords: consciousness centred communication; USP model; Indian philosophy; sphoṭa; pratibhā; meaning formation; reflexivity; human–AI communication

articles.title: Late evolutionary origins of necessary key abilities for true ritual
articles.abstract: Human ritual is difficult to trace directly in deep time. We approach its evolutionary origins indirectly by asking when the necessary cognitive prerequisites for ritual were first plausibly present in the archaeological record – to impose a terminus post quem for true ritual. We argue that true ritual, unlike mere “ritualized” biological behaviour and unlike possible precursors, requires know-how copying: the causal reproduction of behavioural and/or artefactual forms derived from the observation of models, which crucially includes forms that individuals would not realistically perform without having observed such models. Because spontaneous know-how copying in non-human great apes is nearly or completely absent, ritual was probably not inherited from our last common ancestor. We therefore look to the hominin archaeological record. We argue that the earliest stone tools – and especially the Oldowan - did not require know-how copying, and so do not by themselves positively evidence the necessary cognitive capacity required for true ritual. However, this cognitive capacity may become apparent in the middle to late Acheulean, roughly 800,000–500,000 years ago, when knapped stone forms become more diverse and complex, and where their underlying know-how cannot parsimoniously be explained in other ways. That is, the middle to late Acheulean positively evidence for the first type(s) of know-how copying, and as a result, we suggest this period as the earliest plausible window the necessary cognitive faculties required for true ritual. The inferred presence of know-how copying at these times suggests the last common ancestor of humans, Neanderthals and Denisovans, were the first plausible candidates for the earliest true ritual. We leave open the possibility that true ritual may also require symbolism as another key element, though we speculate that symbolism may have emerged more recently, perhaps between 500,000 and 150,000 years ago. If so, full true ritual should be sought mainly within that later bracket. Our dates are not presented as final, but as a cognitive-archaeologically derived guide for narrowing the search. These dates may change in the future with new primatological or archaeological evidence or when new types of analysis become available.

articles.title: Healthism as the ideological substrate of orthorexia nervosa: health, morality, and self-discipline in contemporary food culture
articles.abstract: Orthorexia nervosa (ON), commonly described as a pathological preoccupation with healthy or “pure” eating, has attracted growing attention across psychology, psychiatry, nutrition studies, and the medical humanities. While existing research has predominantly approached orthorexia through individual psychopathology, personality traits, eating behaviors, and diagnostic classification, comparatively less attention has been paid to the ideological environment in which orthorexic practices become meaningful, legitimate, and socially reinforced. This article argues that healthism constitutes an important ideological substrate of orthorexia nervosa. Drawing on Robert Crawford’s concept of healthism and interdisciplinary research on orthorexia, the article conceptualizes orthorexia not simply as an individual fixation on healthy eating but as a potential pathological intensification of culturally normalized imperatives of health optimization. Healthism transforms health from one human value among others into a moral obligation and increasingly locates responsibility for health within individual lifestyle choices. Within this ideological environment, food becomes morally classified, bodily discipline becomes evidence of responsible citizenship, and failure to maintain an “optimal” lifestyle may generate guilt, anxiety, and stigma. Social media and digital wellness cultures can further amplify these processes by circulating idealized representations of clean eating, fitness, bodily control, and self-optimization. The article proposes a conceptual pathway linking healthism, moralization of food, individualization of health responsibility, self-surveillance, dietary restriction, and orthorexic tendencies. It concludes that understanding orthorexia requires attention not only to individual psychological vulnerability but also to the broader sociocultural conditions that normalize obsessive health practices.

articles.title: Two-Person Additively-Separable Sum Games
articles.abstract: We consider a sub-class of bi-matrix games which we refer to as two-person (hereafter referred to as two-player) additively-separable sum (TPASS) games, where the sum of the pay-offs of the two players is additively separable. The row player’s pay-off at each pair of pure strategies, is the sum of two numbers, the first of which may be dependent on the pure strategy chosen by the column player and the second being independent of the pure strategy chosen by the column player. The column player’s pay-off at each pair of pure strategies, is also the sum of two numbers, the first of which may be dependent on the pure strategy chosen by the row player and the second being independent of the pure strategy chosen by the row player. The sum of the inter-dependent components of the pay-offs of the two players is assumed to be zero. We prove the existence of equilibrium for such games and show that the set of equilibria for such games is the projection on the set of strategy pairs of the solutions of a pair of linear programming problem that are dual to each other. This result is a generalization of the corresponding and well-known result for two-person zero-sum games. We also show that a (randomized or mixed) strategy pair is an equilibrium of the game if and only if there exist two other real numbers such that the three together solve a certain linear programming problem. In order to prove this result, we need to appeal to the existence of an equilibrium for the TPASS game. The technology we use to prove our results, consists of the duality theorems and the complementary slackness theorem of linear programming.

articles.title: Hippocampal Neuronal Overflow and Cortical Reconstruction: A Hypothesis on the Formation of Neural Networks Unique to the Human Brain
articles.abstract: This study explores the neural basis of humans’ unique cognitive abilities, focusing on the extensive neuronal migration in white matter that continues for nearly 18 months after birth. Traditional views attribute these migrating neurons to the ventral telencephalon during the fetal period, but this cannot adequately explain their scale and duration. We propose the “Hippocampal Neuronal Overflow and Cortical Reconstruction” hypothesis: hippocampal neurogenesis in human infants peaks perinatally, and under rich environmental stimulation the survival of new hippocampal neurons increases markedly. When their number exceeds the hippocampus’s capacity, they overflow into the white matter and migrate without a fixed route, occupying channels used by normally migrating neurons and displacing them. We term both groups “hippocampal-type neurons.” The depletion of normal neurons from the migration stream may also trigger compensatory proliferation at their source. Hippocampal-type neurons distribute across the frontal, insular, and parietal cortices and parts of the temporal cortex, where they may form a novel neural network. This overflow may be a developmental mechanism unique to humans, and the network may underlie human-specific language, memory transformation, and advanced cognition, offering a new perspective on the uniqueness of human brain development.

articles.title: Team design, best practice, and bad management: Lessons from software development
articles.authors: Ian Hill, Clive Trusson, Matt Vidal
articles.abstract: This article presents a comparative case study examining variation in team design and performance across 13 teams within agile software development. We develop a novel typology of team forms, distinguishing between process autonomy, task autonomy, and authority to contribute to planning and process improvement. This results in four team types: autonomous, semiautonomous, empowered, and manager-led. Ten of the 13 teams were semiautonomous, which was perceived as best practice by most of the 40 managers and developers we interviewed. While nine of the 10 semiautonomous teams regularly and effectively engaged in continuous improvement activities, none of the three manager-led teams did so. We present comparative performance data on ‘sprint’ planning in two teams, which support the hypothesis that semiautonomous teams perform better than manager-led teams. We explain variation in team design as an outcome of managerial satisficing (settling for satisfactory rather than optimal performance) and managerial orientation.

articles.title: Partisan, Geographic, and Demographic Fairness in New Jersey's 2022-2031 Congressional Map
articles.abstract: This study asks whether New Jersey's enacted 2022-2031 congressional map shows measurable partisan bias, meets population-equality and compactness standards, and raises separate demographic concerns. Using 2022 U.S. House returns, the Redistricting Commission's 2020 Census reports, and TIGER/Line boundaries, it computes the efficiency gap, mean-median difference, partisan bias, seats-votes symmetry, Wang's lopsided-margins test, Polsby-Popper and Reock compactness, population deviation, and demographic correlations with vote share. The efficiency gap is +0.091 (about 1.1 of 12 seats), under the roughly two-seat threshold proposed for congressional maps. The mean-median difference (+0.0024) and partisan bias under a mean-of-districts swing (0.00) are near zero; measured from the turnout-weighted statewide vote, partisan bias is +0.25, a real difference driven by lower turnout in packed Democratic districts. On 2020 presidential returns the same two conventions give 0.00 and +0.08, suggesting the 2022 gap is partly a midterm turnout or House-specific candidate effect. Wang's lopsided-margins test is uninformative (p = 0.58). Compactness is low in dense urban districts (Polsby-Popper 0.11-0.39); population deviation is 0.0003% (a two-person range). Nonwhite population share correlates strongly with Democratic vote share (r = 0.85, p < 0.001). Under the mean-of-districts convention the map is close to neutral at a tie; it is highly responsive just above a tie, and least compact on Polsby-Popper in diverse urban districts -- a picture no single metric captures.

articles.title: Clean Water Is a Shared Environmental Priority, Even at Economic Cost
articles.authors: Daniil Romanov, Sergey Utkin, Yaroslav Snarski, Evgeny Sedashov
articles.abstract: Environmental problems rarely respect national borders, and addressing them requires coordinated action across societies with very different economic and institutional conditions. Such coordination requires two things: a shared understanding of which problems matter most, and a willingness to sacrifice some economic well-being to address them. This raises two basic questions: is there common ground in how different societies rank environmental priorities, and are people willing to bear economic costs to address the highest-ranked ones? To answer these questions, we fielded the same paired conjoint experiment in ten countries across diverse world regions (N = 15,123): the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, the Czech Republic, South Korea, Mexico, India, Nigeria, and South Africa. Respondents evaluated hypothetical countries varying in six environmental and three economic conditions. Water quality emerges as the clearest cross-national common denominator, with air quality a consistent second, while agreement on other environmental attributes is weaker. Trade-off analyses show that respondents are willing to accept a weaker national economy in exchange for clean water, a pattern that holds in nine of ten countries, South Korea being the exception. These findings identify a common core within multidimensional environmental preferences.

articles.title: How accurate are app-based farmer self-reports? Evidence from coffee production records in Burundi
articles.authors: Elena Serfilippi, Carlos de los Rios, José Antonio Mendoza Sánchez
articles.abstract: Governments and donors increasingly collect agricultural data through digital tools, but evidence remains limited on how production estimates from farmer-mediated tools compare with those from enumerator surveys. We address this with coffee production data from about 300 farmers in Burundi. Farmers logged sales in a mobile application and answered an end-of-season in-person survey (CAPI); we benchmark both against records from six Coffee Washing Stations where cherry is weighed. App reports fall 21 per cent below the benchmark; the in-person survey stays within 4 per cent. The app's ranking accuracy varies with use: among farmers with above-median participation, the app ranks farmers about as well as the in-person survey (Spearman 0.82 against 0.87, not significant); below the median it does worse (0.60 against 0.83). The shortfall comes from unlogged transactions rather than understated amounts, and it grows with recorded production, so a constant correction cannot remove it. Our results suggest combining the two modes rather than replacing one with the other: app data can rank farmers where use is sustained, but aggregate production figures still require enumerator surveys or administrative records.

articles.title: The Moral–Ethical Technology Acceptance (META) Framework: Understanding Audiences’ Ethical Reasoning and Moral Judgment in the Evaluation of Resurrection Deepfakes
articles.authors: María T. Soto-Sanfiel, Marie Therese Mäder, Gina Junhan Fu
articles.abstract: This study introduces the Moral–Ethical Technology Acceptance (META) framework, a multilevel model integrating the Social Shaping of Technology (SST), the Social Construction of Technology (SCOT), and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), as well as the latter’s Cognitive–Affective–Normative (CAN) extension. META is used to examine how ethical reasoning and moral judgment interact with cognitive, affective, and behavioral responses to emerging technologies. Using a qualitative design, seventy-five university students were invited to reflect on the ethical legitimacy of resurrection deepfakes. Reflexive thematic analysis identified three moral domains under which use was considered legitimate: educational value, emotional or therapeutic benefit, and artistic opportunity. Deepfakes were accepted when perceived as transparent, authentic, and serving the common or affective good, but rejected when they were seen to breach principles of truth, consent, or dignity. The findings confirm that moral judgment and ethical reasoning are integral to how technologies are evaluated and validate META as a transferable model for analyzing how shared values and individual moral judgments shape acceptance in ethically indeterminate technological domains such as synthetic media.

articles.title: Gain Versus Loss Framing in Digital and Visual Persuasive Communication: A Post-2020 Bounded Structured Review and Meta-Analysis of Behavioral Intentions
articles.abstract: This bounded structured review and meta-analysis examined whether messages emphasizing the benefits of acting (gain framing) or the costs of not acting (loss framing) produced stronger behavioral intentions in digital and visual persuasive communication. The search covered January 1, 2021, through September 24, 2026, using four search routes that retained the first 12 retrievable results from each route, combined with an earlier curated set of studies. After deduplication, 79 records were screened, 42 full-text reports were assessed, and 36 reports were included. The quantitative synthesis comprised 12 independent effects from 11 reports (contrast N = 6,851). A REML random-effects model with Hartung–Knapp inference produced g = 0.008, 95% CI [-0.153, 0.168], with substantial heterogeneity, Q(11) = 81.01, p < .001, I² = 86.4%, τ² = 0.0485, and a 95% prediction interval of [-0.503, 0.518]. This near-zero pooled effect indicated that neither framing approach produced stronger behavioral intentions on average. Individual studies varied considerably: Some favored gain framing, some favored loss framing, and many found little difference. Exploratory comparisons found no clear difference between environmental and consumer contexts (p = .445) or between mainland China and other locations (p = .137), but both comparisons were underpowered. Overall, the findings do not support a universal gain- or loss-framing advantage. Instead, framing effects may depend on the audience, behavior, platform, and surrounding message features, although these explanations require stronger comparative evidence.

articles.title: When Communities Lead the Questions: Indigenous-Driven Research on Substance Use, Stigma, and Recovery in Southern California
articles.authors: Alina Ionela Palimaru, Ryan Brown, Rhonda Romero, Vincent Gonzalez, Valerie Aguilar, Robert Aguilar, Tommi Gaines, Carrie Johnson, Elizabeth J. D’Amico
articles.abstract: Background: Indigenous communities hold deep knowledge of what drives substance use, impedes recovery, and constitutes healing—yet this knowledge remains largely absent from the health science knowledge system (HSKS). This study, initiated by Inner-Tribal Treatment (ITT)—Southern California's only Native-led certified substance use program—centers that knowledge through Indigenous Standpoint Theory, engaging ITT's collective expertise and research priorities through co-developed protocols and full analytical participation. Methodology: ITT community researchers conducted 8 focus groups and 16 interviews with 56 participants across 17 Tribes. Analysis proceeded iteratively between community and academic partners, with community interpretation shaping the framework and all findings reviewed by ITT before finalization. Results: Community-generated findings revealed: family enabling as love rooted in intergenerational patterns; the aspirational power of visible recovery in reservation communities; the "sick forest" problem—returning from treatment to unchanged environments without transitional support often leading to relapse; and a paradox in which seeking treatment risks child removal, thereby silencing parents most in need. Conclusions: By centering Indigenous perspectives, this study informs the HSKS by demonstrating that community expertise and lived experiences produce situational knowledge academic approaches alone cannot access. Findings indicate that providing universal access to interventions, strengthening family supports, safeguarding parental rights, and revitalizing cultural identity could help decrease substance use and improve mental health in Indigenous communities. Policy and Practice Implications: Results highlight the importance of redesigning and funding intake systems to eliminate barriers to treatment, facility-level reforms integrating cultural practices throughout the treatment journey rather than as supplements, and child welfare reforms protecting family unity during recovery.

articles.title: Calibration and subgroup fairness of a childhood stunting risk model: a cross-sectional analysis of the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey 2022

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Childhood stunting affects roughly one in four children under five in Bangladesh. Machine learning models are increasingly proposed for risk stratification, but published reports typically emphasise discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, AUROC) and rarely examine calibration or subgroup performance. This study evaluated a stunting risk model on population health survey data, with calibration and subgroup fairness as primary outcomes rather than secondary considerations. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of the 2022 Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) Kids Recode. The outcome was stunting, defined as a height-for-age z-score below -2 standard deviations using the WHO 2006 growth standards. Of 8,784 child records, 13 had implausible anthropometric measurements and 4,666 had missing outcome data, leaving 4,105 children in 670 enumeration areas (weighted prevalence 23.2%). Thirteen predictors were restricted to information plausibly available before anthropometric assessment. A regularised logistic regression was compared with a gradient-boosted tree model (XGBoost). Models were trained on 3,315 children in 536 enumeration areas and evaluated on 790 children in 134 enumeration areas, with no cluster contributing to both arms. Performance was assessed by AUROC, Brier score with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and expected calibration error (ECE) with 10 quantile bins. Subgroup metrics were computed separately by residence, wealth quintile, and sex. A random split was additionally fitted to quantify the cost of ignoring the survey's cluster design. Results: Logistic regression achieved AUROC 0.652, Brier score 0.169 (95% CI 0.154-0.184), and ECE 0.028. XGBoost achieved AUROC 0.651, Brier score 0.171 (0.155-0.187), and ECE 0.043. Discrimination and calibration were similar for rural and urban children (AUROC 0.648 vs 0.660; ECE 0.033 vs 0.032). Within every wealth quintile the model's Brier score was within 0.005 of the base-rate benchmark, indicating no meaningful improvement over predicting the group mean at that level. Discrimination differed by sex: AUROC 0.609 for boys versus 0.692 for girls, with nearly identical calibration (ECE 0.043 vs 0.045). The random-split comparison inflated AUROC by only 0.002, indicating minimal cluster leakage with these individual and household-level predictors. Conclusions: A regularised logistic regression matched a gradient-boosted model on discrimination and calibrated better. The model performed fairly across residence and wealth, but discriminated stunting risk substantially better for girls than for boys. Prediction studies of childhood undernutrition should report calibration and subgroup analyses alongside AUROC, and should evaluate models on held-out clusters when the underlying survey uses a clustered design.

articles.title: Learning to Be Political: Audience Reinforcement and the Disproportionate Political Role of Smaller Social Media Influencers
articles.authors: Christian Pipal, Morgan Wack, Eva-Maria Vogel, Frank Esser
articles.abstract: Some social media influencers (SMIs) occasionally discuss political actors and events, while others regularly engage with political topics. We ask here whether audience response helps explain this difference. We argue that engagement with political posts provides feedback that can reinforce further political posting and, over time, a move toward formal-political content. We test this argument using 761,102 Instagram posts from 1,683 Austrian and German SMIs collected over 60 months (2021–2025), combining a validated two-stage text classification pipeline with within-creator fixed-effects regressions and Cox proportional-hazards models. Political posts receive 18% more likes and 28% more comments than non-political posts by the same creator, although this boost is not larger for smaller creators. A better-performing first political post is followed sooner by another political post. Stronger engagement with lifestyle-political posts also predicts an earlier move into formal-political content, with implications for democracy given the increasing prominence of SMIs as agenda-setters in digital ecosystems. Smaller creators post political content at higher rates. Audience response therefore helps explain why political communication by SMIs persists and how it can move toward formal politics.

articles.title: The Robustness of Political Opinion Bias in Frontier LLMs
articles.authors: Walter Daelemans, stefaan walgrave, Jonas Lefevere
articles.abstract: Citizens increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for political information, yet it remains unclear to what extent these systems are politically biased. This is important as LLMs’ are often used to acquire political information, but such requests can quickly morph into implicit advice—which is then worrisome if the information provided is biased. So, we examine six frontier LLM models and investigate their political opinion bias using 88 statements from the Belgian voting advice application Stemtest, for which the 13 main Belgian parties supplied official answers, and expert-based translations are available. Within a single framework, we test robustness to translation (Dutch, French, English), polarity reversal, explicit persona assignment, and indirect user cues. Responses were analyzed with logistic mixed models on raw repetitions. As expected, all models’ default positions are economically left and culturally progressive, and this position is robust to statement subsampling, translation, and polarity reversal. In contrast, context manipulations shift positions dramatically. Persona assignment moves all models toward the assigned quadrant. More troublesome, we find that user cues, which should not influence a model asked for its own opinion, produce nearly equivalent shifts, indicating sycophancy. These findings suggest that LLMs combine a stable left-progressive default with strong ideological malleability, raising concerns about political advice that reinforces users’ existing views.

articles.title: Misinformation and disinformation strategies of the neoliberal state in Loïc Wacquant’s theory and the potential for resistance among social workers
articles.authors: Barbora Kubatova, Radka Janebová, Daniel Štěpánek, Miroslav Kappl
articles.abstract: Summary: This article examines the neoliberal cultural policies employed in the promotion of social reforms and the mis/disinformation strategies associated with such policies, as delineated in the work of Loïc Wacquant. The objective is to construct an analytical framework that elucidates how symbolic specialists shape public discourse, influence affective responses, and legitimise social inequalities and repressive state measures. Findings: A systematic thematic analysis of Wacquant’s books published between 2001 and 2024 identified six principal strategies: silence concerning structural problems; the politics of emotion; the ideological conditioning of populations; hierarchical categorisation; the mobilisation of the ‘decent’; and the self-affirmation of discourse. These strategies are conceptualised as constituting a cyclical process designed to shape subjectivities and foster the internalisation of neoliberal values. Applications: The proposed model provides social workers with a framework for identifying, deconstructing, and counteracting mis/disinformation strategies that promote neoliberal social reforms. The findings suggest that resistance to neoliberal cultural policy requires a coalition of critical symbolic producers capable of constructing alternative discourses and harnessing emotions of solidarity.

articles.title: When Polarity Silences Distress: From Representational Blind Spots to Task Framings in Mental-Health Inference
articles.abstract: Sentiment polarity is not designed as a measure of psychological distress, but polarity-based features are increasingly used in computational analyses of mental-health text. This creates a construct-validity question: what distress is overlooked when positive-negative tone stands in for a writer's psychological state? We audit sentiment-based inference on 4,420 Reddit posts from five mental-health communities, moving from VADER to DistilBERT and Twitter-RoBERTa, then to a zero-shot classifier and two newer generative models, pairing quantitative scoring with qualitative analysis and dual coding. Category means differed significantly, but condition explained only 1.6% of the variance. The audit surfaces recurring cases in which contextually recognizable distress is scored positive. We call this mismatch the Silencing Effect and organize it into a four-part taxonomy of representational blind spots: the Somatic Representation Gap, Affective Blunting Gap, Discourse Masking Gap, and Variance Masking Gap. Contextual models reclassified most keyword-screened candidates, but 24 posts remained non-negative across all three valence-based models; 22 were judged distressed by both coders. On these 22 posts, recovery varied from 72.7% to 100% across five task framings within the same zero-shot model. Holding posts fixed while changing the task target reveals that recovery depends on what the model is asked to judge, not only on what the text contains. Two generative models preserved the same top-two ranking with a smaller spread, and the best person-anchored framing recovered all 22 posts in all three models. Polarity contains useful information about distress but is not interchangeable with person-level psychological state. Sentiment outputs should not be read as direct measures of distress without construct-specific validation.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Financial Services in India: Adoption, Risks, Regulation and the Future of Fintech Lending
articles.authors: Tanushree Kaushal, Monami Dasgupta, Sugandh Saxena, Saishya Duggal
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping India’s financial services sector, with fintech (digital) lending emerging as a key area of adoption. Built on the country’s large-scale digital public infrastructure, digital lenders increasingly deploy AI across the credit lifecycle. These tools promise to widen formal credit access for new-to-credit and thin-file borrowers, micro and small enterprises, gig workers and low-to-mid-income households. However, they also raise concerns about algorithmic transparency, explainability, discrimination, consumer protection, privacy and cybersecurity. India has no single AI-specific law and oversight instead follows the sector-led, “techno-legal” approach set out in MeitY’s India AI Governance Guidelines (2025), which channels oversight through regulators such as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). This report draws on structured interviews with industry leaders and technology vendors, together with a survey of 21 digital lending firms which are estimated to account for roughly 80% of digital lending volume in the country. The report maps trends in AI adoption, identifies operational and governance challenges, and assesses future trajectories. Firms see productivity gains but cannot yet attribute profitability to AI, which leaves the business case unproven even as investment intentions grow, particularly in collections and customer experience. The most significant risks are data quality, cybersecurity and dependence on third-party vendors. India relies on sector-led, principles-based oversight, and the RBI’s draft model risk guidance is not yet binding, so regulatory ambiguity persists. The central challenge is to extend governance outward to customers, vendors and data supply chains, as quickly as deployment advances.

articles.title: How Can Non-Governmental Organisations and Civil Society Groups Support an Effective International Prohibition Regime? Perspectives Following Two Review Conferences
articles.authors: Lalitha Sundaram, Alexandra Klein, Tom Hobson, Catherine Rhodes

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Non-governmental organisations and civil society groups have had a growing presence at the Biological Weapons Convention Review Conferences over the last few decades, with participation growing from six individuals in 1980 to more than 170 registered participants at the most recent Review Conference in 2022. This chapter draws on two workshops hosted by the University of Cambridge’s Centre for the Study of Existential Risk in the aftermath of the Eighth and Ninth Review Conferences respectively. These workshops brought together academic and policy experts from disarmament and non-proliferation, the biosciences, and biosecurity to discuss the outcomes of the conferences and how these might shape the role of civil society efforts to support the aims of the Convention, especially in light of disappointing formal progress. In this chapter, we put forward several areas in which the workshops revealed unmet needs and suggest ways in which civil society might be able to contribute. These are grouped under the themes: Conflict, Consensus and Political Will; Resourcing and Representativeness; Scope and Extent of the Convention; and Knowledge Sharing, Expertise and Analysis. We end with reflections on how the focus of civil society work may change in response to possible future scenarios for the BWC.

articles.title: “Why Do Women Steal Away Men's Joy?" – A Qualitative Content Analysis of Manfluencers’ Discourse on YouTube Short Content
articles.authors: Matteo Rinaldi, Freya De Keyzer, Simone Driessen, Julia Kneer
articles.abstract: The rise of social media platforms has facilitated both positive democratic engagement and the spread of toxic, gendered-divisive discourse. Within this landscape, the "manosphere" has evolved into an ecosystem where influencers, or "manfluencers," share misogynistic, polarizing, views. While prior research has examined manosphere discourse mostly in text-based forms, limited attention has been paid to how it is articulated in short video content (SVC), such as YouTube Shorts. To investigate this, this study employed a qualitative content analysis via a Visual-Verbal Video Analysis (VVVA) and a discourse analysis of speech and design alike. Findings were analyzed to explore, describe, and organize the various general, visual, multimodal, character, and compositional elements of manfluencers’ content, increasing engagement and virality on social media platforms. Results indicated that manfluencers expressed toxicity through discourse, using SVC multimodal design phenomena to maximize the sharing of their values and ideas. They used not only specific language, elements (e.g. win/lose and business-lingo), and styles (e.g. podcast debates, sketch comedy, etc.) to convey their messages, but also strategically combined them with specific multimodal design phenomena (e.g. zoom, cuts, music, etc.) to reinforce certain views over others.

articles.title: MODELING REVENUE PERFORMANCE IN COMMERCIAL AVIATION: A MULTI‑MODEL ANALYSIS OF PUBLIC SENTIMENT, REVENUE METRICS, AND MACROECONOMIC INDICATORS
articles.abstract: Social media has intensified the visibility and impact of customer reactions, making corporate reputation increasingly sensitive to the rapid spread of online sentiment. This study investigates the relationship between social media sentiment and airline revenue performance using the United Airlines passenger removal incident of April 2017 as a case study. Specifically, it evaluates whether sentiment changes correspond with variations in Passenger Revenue per Available Seat Mile (PRASM) and passenger Yield, controlling for key operational and macroeconomic factors. A Large Language Model (LLM)–based sentiment analysis approach was used to extract, classify, and quantify social media sentiment related to United Airlines. Monthly and quarterly normalized sentiment scores were integrated with publicly available financial and operational indicators, including PRASM, Yield, Passenger Revenue, Available Seat Miles (ASM), Revenue Passenger Miles (RPM), U.S. GDP growth, and seasonal demand. Multiple linear regression models were used to assess the relationship between sentiment and revenue performance. Results show that public sentiment is a statistically significant predictor of both PRASM and Yield. Both sentiment and GDP exhibited significant positive effects on Yield. These findings indicate that favorable public sentiment enhances airline revenue performance by strengthening pricing power and revenue efficiency, while macroeconomic conditions and seasonal demand also play important roles. The study provides empirical evidence that social media sentiment is a valuable non financial indicator of airline performance and should complement traditional operational and economic metrics in revenue management and forecasting.

articles.title: Beware of broadstancing: Minoritised politicians broadening their electoral appeal by distancing themselves from their ascribed in-group
articles.abstract: Many observers of politics will recognise cases of minoritised politicians distancing themselves from their in-group. This is often received as a surprising exception to the assumed rule that minoritised politicians will stand for the interests of their ascribed in-group members. I argue that this phenomenon is not an exception, but instead, the rule in most electoral contexts. Drawing on research based on gender, ethnic, racial, religious and sexual diversity in politics, I introduce the term broadstancing to describe when minoritised politicians broaden their electoral appeal by distancing themselves from their ascribed in-group. I map the distinct dynamics that cause broadstancing across various electoral contexts. Instead of understanding broadstancing as a surprising phenomenon, I conceptualise it as a logical dynamic that leverages the onlooker’s initial surprise to reinforce political inequalities. Broadstancing veils policies that reduce equality, it legitimises narratives and practices that would otherwise attract (more) criticism, and softens the tone of exclusionary practices. I argue that the public needs to understand this logic of representation to safeguard the healthy functioning of democracy.

articles.title: The Decline of Identity Voting? Politicians' Socio-Demographic Characteristics and Voter Attitudes and Behaviour
articles.abstract: This chapter reviews and reconsiders the relationship between politicians’ social identities and voting behaviour. A long tradition of research shows that voters’ evaluations of politicians’ traits, beliefs, and competences are influenced by stereotypes about politicians’ identities, such as gender, sexuality, class, disability, race/ethnicity, and religion, as well as the intersections between them. Yet, more recent evidence suggests that voter bias, where voters are less likely to vote for candidates from certain groups, is either limited or highly conditional on ideology, context, and the activation of stereotypes, challenging earlier assumptions that candidates with certain identities were inherently disadvantaged in elections. At the same time, political parties, particularly on the Right, have increasingly diversified their candidate pools, even where electoral incentives to do so seem limited. We argue that these trends are unlikely to signify a decline in the importance of personality politics; rather, both politicians and parties are strategic about their use and framing of politicians’ identities. Politicians from marginalised groups strategically distance themselves from group-associated positions to expand their electoral appeal. Parties include marginalised groups among decision-makers to either lend credibility to policies benefitting these groups or legitimise policies that may undermine group interests. Understanding how marginalised identities are mobilised in political competition is essential not only for advancing scholarly debates on representation, but also for informing public awareness of the instrumentalisation of identities and mitigating the normalisation of exclusionary policies.

articles.title: The Second Decision: Where Early Retention Loss Falls in YouTube Shorts
articles.abstract: Every time you watch a short-form video, you make two decisions: whether to stop scrolling and whether to keep watching. On YouTube, the first decision shows up as a metric called “Stayed to watch”. The second shows up as a metric called retention, which can be visualized by the retention curve: the share of the audience still watching at each moment. Two short-form videos could have the same retention, holding viewers equally well overall, but still lose them at different moments. Does that matter? Most Shorts are experience goods (Nelson, 1970): you only learn if one is worth watching by actually watching it; I ask whether where viewers quit is associated with how well a video performs. I analyzed 2,597 Shorts from 11 channels and three creators, including my own channel, GabeSweats (2M+ subscribers). I measured where each video’s early dropoff (viewers leaving within 1–30% of runtime) happened, and compared that with its views per day. On “promise” channels, videos open by promising, directly or indirectly, to explain or close some gap in information (say, “who is the smartest person ever?”, which promises... well, you get it). On these channels, a bigger share of dropoff between 10–20% of the video’s runtime was associated with fewer views per day. Within the same channel, adjusting for length, year and average retention, a typical difference (one standard deviation) went with about 39% fewer views per day (partial r = −0.28, N = 1,734; −0.17 with the strictest controls). Losing people at the start of a video was surprisingly associated with more views, while losing them after the 20% mark was mostly unrelated. On “format” channels—where you know what you’re getting, like a channel that posts almost nothing but clips from the same TV show—the same link originally showed up under the simplest comparisons, but under the strictest controls, the link nearly disappeared (−0.05). Much of the promise result comes from just two of the eleven channels, and by nature this is an observational study and does not establish causality.

articles.title: Changing Winds: Central Bank Independence, An Institutionalist Analysis

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The European Central Bank, Federal Reserve and Bank of England enjoy broad and extensive power to determine monetary policy. Yet how exactly do they function, and what mandate do they have over monetary policy? On what epistemological roots does their path-dependent development rest? Given that they are independent from direct political intervention, how can they be held accountable and retain their legitimacy, and what are the consequences when either is lacking? This paper addresses these questions through the lens of institutional economics, through a qualitative historical-institutional analysis of documents produced by the central banks themselves and by political actors engaging with them. It argues that the post-2008 period has produced a structural rather than transitional mismatch between the institutional design of central bank independence and the role central banks now perform in practice. Their legal mandates have remained largely unchanged, yet the practical operation of those mandates has expanded substantially under crisis conditions. This expansion of de facto authority has not been matched by a corresponding development of democratic accountability mechanisms, producing a legitimacy deficit that is increasingly visible in political contestation across the US, the EU, and the UK.

articles.title: Musical Genes: A Conceptual Framework for Culturally Informed Feature Extraction in Traditional Music
articles.abstract: Feature extraction in traditional music requires decisions about which relations to compare, which variations preserve the identity of an analytical unit, and what cultural interpretations the resulting features can support. Drawing on culturally situated information modeling and cross-cultural similarity research, this article develops a conceptual framework through conceptual analysis, a purposive synthesis of the literature, and qualitative reanalysis of selected score excerpts. The term ‘musical gene’ connects two claims about the same candidate unit: that it retains its structural identity across realizations and that it is transmitted through cultural practice. Each claim requires corresponding evidence. A three-layer model distinguishes core structure, realization, and contextual constraints. A six-step procedure defines units for specific tasks, specifies data fields such as register, part, position, and provenance, and assesses structural, perceptual, and transmission claims separately. Hezhou Daling illustrates how register informs the description of a tonal pattern. A pedagogical comparison of a Dong cicada-song excerpt shows which data are needed to distinguish part pairings. Both cases identify supported judgments, inferences requiring revision or withdrawal, and claims awaiting further evidence. The framework links feature selection, encoding, and interpretation through traceable records, clarifying when a musical-gene claim is warranted and when a general feature description remains appropriate. Keywords: musical gene; musical traditions; feature extraction; analytical unit; quantitative research; cultural transmission

articles.title: Borrower Age and ARM Selection: 2023 HMDA Evidence
articles.abstract: This paper examines whether a borrower’s age affects their choice of mortgage, even after accounting for factors such as expected income growth and how often they may move. Using nationwide mortgage data from 2021, 2023, and 2024, I study four types of mortgage features that can offer lower monthly payments: adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), interest-only loans, extended-amortization loans, and balloon-payment loans. Following the Dodd-Frank mortgage reforms, all but ARMs have become relatively uncommon. In 2023 and 2024, when interest rates were high, ARMs were the most common of these four features in all 50 states and Washington, D.C. However, in 2021, when interest rates were low, ARMs were the most common in only 43 states, while interest-only loans were more common in the remaining eight. After accounting for factors such as income, loan size, loan program, expected mobility, and differences between states and lenders, I find that age still plays a role in mortgage selection. However, the results are different from my original hypothesis. I expected younger borrowers with greater financial constraints to be more likely to choose mortgages with lower monthly payments. Instead, the strongest relationships appear among older borrowers who seem to have greater financial flexibility, especially for balloon-payment loans. The relationship between older age and ARM selection appears in all three years, regardless of whether interest rates were high or low. In contrast, the results for borrowers under 35 are less consistent across the years. These findings suggest that financial difficulties among younger borrowers do not fully explain why people choose these mortgage features. One possible explanation is that older borrowers expect to move or pay off their loans sooner. Another is that they prefer lower monthly payments even when they can afford higher ones. Differences in financial knowledge and experience may also influence mortgage choices. However, more research is needed to determine why these patterns occur.

articles.title: Retrofitting, densification and nature-based solutions in Paris and Orléans: Stakeholder scenario mapping (ReHousIn Deliverable 5.2, France)
articles.authors: Federica Rotondo, Sarah Bouchafa, Marco Cremaschi, Tommaso Vitale, Antoine Guirronet

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This empirical report presents the results of three stakeholder scenario-mapping workshops held in June 2026 in Paris and Orléans as part of the Horizon Europe project ReHousIn (Deliverable 5.2). For the interpretive synthesis of the French case and its European comparison, see Cremaschi, Guironnet, Rotondo and Vitale (2026), doi:10.31235/osf.io/ynkcr_v1. The workshops brought together municipal and metropolitan administrations, public development agencies, social housing providers, private developers and housing support organisations to examine the distributive effects of three green housing interventions: housing retrofitting combined with nature-based solutions in Paris and in Orléans, and densification through land recycling in the Paris region. For each case, the report reconstructs the key impacts, the mechanisms that explain them and the variations across scenarios, then outlines pathways towards just futures, with their levers and trade-offs. Findings show that energy savings from retrofitting are modest and unevenly shared: social housing tenants benefit most, while low-income owner-occupiers in condominiums face upfront costs with payback periods of 20 to 30 years, longer than their expected tenure, which can push them to sell. Densification generates amenities but mainly raises property values, with gains captured by surrounding owners and displacement risks for private tenants. In Orléans, one-for-one demolition rules have led to de-densification. The report identifies policy levers (rent regulation, deferred-repayment advances for low-income owners, public land control, developer charters, regulatory stability) and two non-negotiable principles: no displacement of lower-income residents because of works, and no rise in housing costs without support for vulnerable households.

articles.title: A Needs-Finding Framework for understanding gaps in Sickle Cell Disease Care Pathway
articles.authors: Kirthana Warrier, Mannat Kuhar, Yash Miryala, Megha Agrawal, Deepa Bhat, Anurag Mairal
articles.abstract: Background: Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) is a genetic blood disorder caused by a point mutation in the HBB gene that replaces glutamic acid with valine, altering the structure of hemoglobin. Unlike healthy, flexible red blood cells, these sickled cells are rigid and prone to clumping in small blood vessels, blocking blood flow and causing pain, tissue damage, and oxygen deprivation. As a result, individuals with SCD experience chronic anemia, fatigue, and delayed physical development. SCD diagnosis and treatment advancements have not been implemented equitably across all settings. Innovation priorities may be weakened when solutions are selected before population needs are defined and prioritized. Objective: The current studies in SCD available in public domain lack a systematic and structured approach to distill key reasons/themes why SCD diagnosis, treatment and management have not achieved substantial success when public health is concerned, even though there have been significant scientific advances in understanding the disease pathophysiologically. The main objective of this study is to identify and prioritize solution-neutral unmet needs in SCD diagnosis, management and treatment by adapting the Stanford Biodesign needs-finding framework to the systematic review of research publications on SCD. Study Design: The Biodesign framework consists of 3 phases: Identify, where needs finding and needs screening occurs; Invent, where the concept generation and filtering occurs; and Implement, where stages for strategy development and prototyping occur prior to the project launch. Needs Finding in Stanford Biodesign framework consists of three primary components: secondary background research, clinician and stakeholder discussions, and on-field observations. In this phase of research, we focused on the first part - secondary background research. The research involved identifying published literature on SCD, with a focus on gaps and unmet needs in SCD care in underserved settings. Deeper review with thematic analysis led to identification of key challenges and gaps in SCD care which formed the basis for writing structured need statements following the Stanford Biodesign template. Framework Results: The study produced 12 priority needs that fall under 4 major themes namely barriers to care, trust and emotional support, early diagnosis / screening and education and awareness. Increased screening needs received the highest total score (20.0) across the 4 criteria. Barriers to care and trust and emotional support received the second highest total score of 19.0. Education and awareness received a total score of 15.0. Conclusion: The Biodesign framework enabled a structured review to convert research evidence into prioritized SCD need statements that warrant solutions. The study identified screening needs, overcoming barriers to care, building trust and emotional support and education and awareness initiatives as the prioritized unmet needs in SCD patients.

articles.title: “When they go low, we kick them”: The reciprocal nature of citizens’ support for democratic transgressions
articles.authors: Lisa Janssen, Anna Kern, Hannah Wernere
articles.abstract: This study examines how citizens respond to democratic transgressions by political opponents and whether they, in turn, support reciprocal transgressions by their own party. Drawing on psychological theories of negative reciprocity, we argue that commitment to democratic principles is relational, shaped by the (un)democratic behavior of other political actors. Through survey experiments in England (N = 4,040) and the United States (N = 4,084) we find that exposure to opponents’ transgressions doubles citizens’ likelihood of endorsing undemocratic actions by their own party. Moreover, we document that tendencies to reciprocate transgressions are independent of citizens’ affective polarization levels. Thematic analyses of open responses (N = 907) reveal that many justify reciprocal transgressions as morally necessary to restore fairness and protect democracy. As such, our findings highlight the need for an interactive approach that captures the dynamic and morally complex nature of citizens’ attitudes towards democratic violations.

articles.title: Harmony Beyond Hedonia and Eudaimonia
articles.abstract: Recent advances in wellbeing research emphasize its multifaceted nature, traditionally defined by hedonic and eudaimonic approaches. However, growing cross-cultural and empirical studies suggest this dichotomy may be insufficient to capture the diversity and complexity of human flourishing. This study investigates harmony as a distinct and essential dimension of wellbeing beyond life satisfaction and meaning in life. Drawing on data from culturally diverse samples in the United States and Hong Kong, confirmatory factor analysis and exploratory structural equation modeling were applied to compare one-, two-, and three-factor models encompassing life satisfaction, meaning in life, and harmony. Across both samples, the three-factor exploratory structural equation modeling model showed the best fit, supporting the empirical distinctiveness of harmony. The findings provide strong empirical evidence for a tripartite model of wellbeing and support harmony as a core dimension of wellbeing. The results underscore the importance of expanding wellbeing frameworks to include culturally sensitive constructs and suggest a more holistic and integrative approach to conceptualizing and operationalizing wellbeing —one that moves beyond the hedonic–eudaimonic dichotomy— and opens new directions for future research, measurement, and interventions. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

articles.title: From Data to Decisions: Applying Inferential Statistics to Idiographic Longitudinal N-of-1 Data to Evaluate Intervention Effects – A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Felicitas Kininger, Simon Blackwell, Julia Glombiewski, Saskia Scholten
articles.abstract: Objective: This scoping review systematically maps analytical methods for evaluating intervention-related change in idiographic longitudinal N-of-1 data from AB single-case experimental designs (SCEDs) and compares their assumptions, data requirements, interpretability, and clinical applicability. Method: Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, we searched six databases from inception to May 2026 for peer-reviewed English-language studies that introduced, compared, or evaluated methods capable of determining the presence or absence of an intervention effect in idiographic or non-standardized outcomes. Methods were charted by methodological characteristics, assumptions, data requirements, clinical applicability, limitations, and software availability. Selected methods were illustrated using daily stress ratings from one clinical AB-SCED and an artificially reduced weekly dataset. Results: We identified 17 methods across 27 papers, comprising visually oriented, nonoverlap, Bayesian, simulation-based, and further approaches. No method was universally suitable. Nonoverlap indices were comparatively accessible but differed in sensitivity to trends, autocorrelation, phase length, and small samples. Bayesian and simulation-based methods offered additional inferential flexibility but required stronger assumptions or expertise. In the case illustration, methods yielded divergent classifications of improvement, deterioration, or no change; most conclusions were stable after weekly subsampling, although Bayes Factor trend evidence and statistical significance for Tau and simulation modelling analysis were attenuated. Conclusions: Method selection should be driven by the clinical question, expected effect pattern, phase length, baseline trend, autocorrelation, measurement properties, interpretability, and implementation resources. Transparent decision procedures combining visual analysis with complementary evidence on change, magnitude, and clinical relevance are needed.

articles.title: Criminal Expertise and Hacking Efficiency
articles.authors: Asier Moneva, Stijn Ruiter, Daniel Meinsma
articles.abstract: Criminal expertise plays a crucial role in the choices offenders make when committing a crime, including their modus operandi. However, our knowledge about criminal decision making online remains limited. Drawing on insights from cyber security, we conceptualize the cybercrime commission process as the sequence of phases of the cyber kill chain that offenders go through. We assume that offenders who follow the sequence consecutively use the most efficient hacking method. Building upon the expertise paradigm, we hypothesize that participants with greater hacking experience and IT skills undertake more efficient hacks. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed data from 69 computer security and software engineering students who were invited to hack a vulnerable website in a computer lab equipped with monitoring software, which allowed to collect objective behavioral measures. Additionally, we collected individual measures regarding hacking expertise through an online questionnaire. After quantitatively measuring efficiency using sequence analysis, a regression model showed that the expertise paradigm may also apply to hackers. We discuss the implications of our novel research for the study of offender decision-making processes more broadly.

articles.title: Doing Wrong in the Name of Good
articles.abstract: Some unjust actions are carried out by people who understand them as right, necessary, or morally obligatory. The injustice remains hidden from the one who harms, although it may be recognized by those harmed or by third parties. The argument developed here explains this modality of wrongdoing as a cycle with three moments. Influences offer an interpreted world; an understanding formed under those influences presents the violation of another person as protection, reparation, or duty; the action so authorized can return as a new influence that reinforces the understanding that made it possible. Once formed, an understanding can come to select the sources it admits, to bind itself to the agent's belonging and self-image, and to reinterpret contrary information as confirmation of the perceived threat. Three documented episodes test the model: the attacks on asylum hotels and a mosque in England after the Southport killings of July 2024, the assault on the United States Capitol on 6 January 2021, and the invasion of the seats of the three branches of government in Brasília on 8 January 2023. In each, participants invoked a good — the protection of children, the defense of the constitution, the salvation of the nation — to authorize harm against persons who had done nothing to them. The model is defended against four objections and completed by a normative criterion that does not depend on the agent's conviction: the person affected remains a participant in a shared condition, and the consideration owed to them is not cancelled by disagreement. On that basis, the final part proposes where and how the cycle can be interrupted: at the moment of influence, at the moment of understanding, and at the moment of action, with a criminal response that arrives late, remains limited, and never reproduces the exclusion it answers.

articles.title: Rebranding the Transnational Illiberal Right: NatCon and the Making of a ‘Conservative International’
articles.abstract: Despite stark differences, diverse right-wing actors have been building a movement that transcends national borders and defies conventional labels. Using the ‘transnational illiberal right-wing movement’ as a working analytical category broader than ‘far right’ or ‘New Right’, we analyze international right-wing conferences to reconstruct the political logic behind the movement and examine social semiotic practices informing political identification with it. Combining Discourse Studies with topic modelling and socio-semantic network analysis, we study the 2024 NatCon Brussels conference as the most likely case for exploring how politicians, intellectuals, and activists engage with the movement and NatCon, one of its key networks, in the EU. We show that, despite the ideological heterogeneity of its participants, the conference was structured around discourses on Europe and conservatism in an attempt to build and ideationally equip an illiberal right-wing electoral coalition before the 2024 European elections. Functioning as a site of hegemonic articulation, the conference enabled its participants to appropriate the signifier ‘conservatism’, presenting the movement as a natural continuation of the conservative tradition while symbolically excluding conservatives portrayed as incompatible with it. The article shows how studying one purposefully selected international conference can illuminate the composition, ideological boundaries, networks, and purposes of such gatherings.

articles.title: A Vote That Did Not Exist: Favelas, Violence, and Change between Rounds in Brazil’s 2026 Presidential Election
articles.abstract: This article examines the spatial distribution of Lula’s vote gains between the two rounds of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election. Using electoral-section results and data from the 2022 Census, we estimate the composition of the electorate at 3,478 polling places in Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. In both cities, Lula made greater gains at polling places with a higher estimated share of favela residents, even after controlling for income, violence, and first-round results. The difference associated with moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile of this share was approximately one percentage point of the registered electorate. In São Paulo, proximity to favelas was also positively associated with Lula’s gains, while Flávio Bolsonaro’s gains were smaller in areas with higher levels of violence in both cities. The comparison with 2022 shows that the association between electorate composition and Lula’s gains intensified in both metropolitan centers. Extending the analysis to 23 large cities shows a smaller intensification on average, distinguishable from zero in only five of them. In 2026, the differential was larger in cities whose state governments elected in 2022 were allied with Bolsonaro. This pattern is consistent with a reaction to security policies, although the aggregate data cannot identify this mechanism or reconstruct individual vote transfers.

articles.title: The Efficacy Loop: Reciprocal Adaptation between Citizens and Conversational AI in Political Judgement
articles.abstract: Research on conversational AI and politics has largely examined two directions of influence separately: how AI shapes citizens’ political attitudes and judgement, and how users’ characteristics and self-presentation shape the responses AI gives them. This article theorises how the two become coupled through epistemic efficacy, a person’s perceived capacity to understand an issue, weigh the evidence and reach a judgement of their own. How capable users present themselves as being may condition the assistance they receive, and that assistance may in turn update how capable they feel, conditioning the next interaction. The central distinction is between assistance that scaffolds political judgement, supporting users as they evaluate evidence and trade-offs for themselves, and assistance that substitutes for it, performing that evaluative work on their behalf. Drawing on an account of epistemic autonomy as governed dependence, the article treats neither as inherently good or bad and assesses assistance by whether it leaves users meaningful control over their judgement. Scaffolding may build confidence in line with the judgement users exercise, whereas substitution may increase reliance and, particularly when combined with validation of the user, raise confidence beyond competence. The article separates efficacy from attitude certainty, explains why AI conclusions differ from conventional political cues, and states falsifiable propositions for each link of the loop. The resulting dynamics have implications for epistemic autonomy and for democratic inequality, because citizens may differ in whether the assistance they receive leaves political judgement in their own hands.

articles.title: Is it Okay to Use Generative AI in Sociological Research?
articles.authors: Oscar Stuhler, Dustin S. Stoltz, AJ Alvero, Marshall A. Taylor
